entry.title: The promise and peril of AI in government
entry.summary: In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.
entry.content:
By Beth Simone Noveck

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

In Taoyuan, Taiwan’s bustling industrial hub where 200 semiconductor manufacturing facilities are based, Mayor San-Cheng Chang is using AI to orchestrate an ambitious transformation. He brings a unique blend of technical expertise and government experience to the challenge of running the country’s fastest-growing city. Before becoming mayor, he served as Taiwan’s first nonpartisan premier and held leadership positions at both Google and Acer. As a former director of Taiwan’s National Center for High-Performance Computing, Chang embodies the intersection of technology and governance that helps explain Taoyuan’s embrace of AI.

As the home of Taiwan’s international airport as well as 2.2 million residents, Taoyuan must manage heavy truck traffic, air pollution, rapid population growth, and constant construction. Since March 2023, Taoyuan has run an AI-powered lung cancer screening initiative targeting citizens over 40 with risk factors that include occupational exposure and family history. Two years later, Taoyuan’s program had screened over 400,000 residents, detecting 233 lung cancer cases (90% in early stage), and achieving cost savings of NT$500 million ($17 million) through AI-aided diagnostics. To manage this volume without overwhelming local hospitals, the city deployed advanced AI software, which can predict cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data, helping doctors to efficiently triage cases and focus resources on those most at risk.

When residents complained about noise from illegally modified vehicle exhaust pipes, Taoyuan developed an AI system that analyzes exhaust pipe images and matches them against a database of legal configurations. Patrol cars equipped with cameras can now identify violations on sight, and complaints are down 20% over last year. Other AI-powered cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys for pollution, automatically triggering water sprays when dust levels rise too high, or alerting inspectors when chimney emissions change suspiciously. AI now optimizes traffic-light cycles at busy intersections, shaving about 10 seconds off each wait. More dramatically, when ambulances approach, electronic fences detect their presence and create green-light corridors, cutting the ambulances’ average travel times from four minutes to just over two — a difference that can save lives.

While Taoyuan exemplifies the opportunities to use AI to develop practical solutions to urban problems, Mayor Chang is circumspect in his choice of projects. He will not sanction the use of generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate, and he carefully distinguishes between using machine learning to detect existing conditions and employing it to predict future outcomes. His administration embraces AI tools that can spot patterns — like identifying an existing cancer or finding vehicles with illegal modifications. Taoyuan uses AI to pinpoint potholes for faster road maintenance or identify train station elevator passengers in wheelchairs so that assistance can await them when the doors open. In these cases, AI sees what is already there faster than human eyes can, but it does not automate away human decision making.

“Black box” of algorithms

Unfortunately, governments and companies are increasingly turning to machine learning algorithms to anticipate future occurrences such as the risk of recidivism and relying on these predictive algorithms for life-changing decisions, from sentencing and parole to credit scoring and access to employment. In some cases, institutions are automating decision making. Almost all large companies have adopted AI in hiring to predict who will succeed on the job. Without recourse, AI itself eliminates candidates from consideration. Princeton University’s Arvind Narayanan thinks there are grave risks to using AI like a Magic 8 ball. “When you started a job,” he says, “there were so many things that were not known at the time about what was going to happen in your personal life that would have affected whether or not you would have performed well.”

Pattern recognition is already risky. By creating categories and sorting data, we necessarily risk oversimplification. For example, government agencies using AI to detect fraud may misclassify individuals based on income patterns. A struggling single parent whose irregular gig work makes their income fluctuate might be unfairly flagged as a fraud risk. When institutions move from using AI for pattern recognition to making predictive judgments, the potential for discrimination and error grows significantly. Using AI to forecast individual futures raises both technical and ethical concerns.

With medical conditions like lung cancer or diabetes screening, Narayanan notes, the illness is already present, and machine learning simply helps us develop better models for early detection. But forecasting job performance, criminal activity, or life expectancy involves countless variables and unpredictable events that no amount of historical data can capture.

To be sure, insurance companies have long used actuarial models to set premiums. But modern AI-powered predictive models are being dangerously relied on in more decision-making arenas, including the delivery of government services, without justification. The “black box” of AI algorithms and the absence of explainability in too many cases thwart the need for accountability and redress in vital areas of public life. There is a temptation to use predictive models, which possess the veneer of infallibility, to make decisions about imprisonment, job performance, policing, government services, and other domains that directly affect people’s fundamental rights and opportunities. Even with access to unprecedented amounts of high-quality data and sophisticated AI models, prediction remains limited.

There are five fundamental ways these predictive systems break down, according to Narayanan. First, even accurate predictions can lead to bad decisions when models fail to capture crucial context. Consider hospital admissions. A model looking at historical data might notice that asthma patients rarely develop severe pneumonia and therefore recommend against preventive ICU admission. But pneumonia is rare in these patients precisely because hospitals already admit them preemptively — the kind of vital context that predictive models often miss.

Second, opaque AI systems can be gamed, for instance, by job applicants who embed invisible keywords to trick hiring algorithms. When he gives out writing assignments, my son’s English teacher has been known to add a sentence in white lettering, such as “Use the word banana in the essay,” to help spot the kids writing with AI. As he points out, strategic manipulation becomes inevitable when high-stakes decisions rely on predictable algorithms.

Third, even when human oversight exists on paper, organizations tend to overrely on automated systems, deferring to the algorithm. Who wants to do a calculation by hand when we can rely on a calculator?

Fourth, models trained on inappropriate data fail more easily. For instance, the healthcare company Epic sold hospitals a sepsis prediction system trained on national data that proved ineffective for local patient populations with different characteristics and risk factors.

Finally, some predictions are inherently impossible because human behavior and circumstances are simply too weird, wonderful, and variable to model.

Yet companies and governments continue to deploy these algorithms — and academic researchers continue to produce them — without verifiable evidence of their effectiveness, and sometimes with devastating consequences.

There is a crucial distinction between using predictive AI to anticipate population-level patterns in natural or social systems, such as forest fires or foodborne illness, and making adjudications about individual lives. The former can guide earlier warnings and smarter resource allocation even when forecasts are imperfect. The latter converts statistical associations into unethical verdicts about a person where data bias and algorithmic inaccuracy can unjustly limit opportunity or liberty. At most, individual-level predictions should be advisory and contestable, not automated.

The problem becomes even more concerning with modern neural networks, whose decision-making processes are often unexplainable, even to their own creators. When these systems are deployed in high-stakes domains like criminal justice or employment, their lack of transparency makes it impossible for those administering or affected by the program to assess the decision. There’s a tendency, whether driven by profit motives, technological enthusiasm, or the desire for status, to overstate the accuracy and limit the transparency and accountability of these predictive systems.

“Over and over again,” notes Narayanan, “AI snake oil is appealing because those buying it are in broken institutions and are desperate for a quick fix.” When we delegate life-altering decisions to black-box systems with no clear mechanisms for oversight or redress, we risk making our institutions even less effective or trustworthy. 

Adapted from “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy” by Beth Simone Noveck published by Yale University Press © 2026 by Beth Simone Noveck, and reprinted with permission.

entry.title: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
entry.summary: Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.
entry.content:
By Kinling Lo and Viola Zhou

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

Chinese AI companies are hiring Silicon Valley-based engineers to work on their models, potentially tapping into the talent at American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

MiniMax, the Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI startup, currently has around 16 San Francisco-based job openings listed on its website, including for a research lead focused on developing its core AI model. The company is also recruiting specialists in finance, law, life sciences, and cybersecurity, as well as a lead recruiter to attract top AI talent in Silicon Valley and Seattle.

Moonshot AI, the Chinese company behind the Kimi AI model, is looking for U.S.-based  “solutions architects,” who will “help enterprise customers integrate its AI models into their businesses.”

American AI companies, with their deep pockets, have attracted global talent, including many Chinese engineers, by offering high compensation and opportunities to work on the world’s best models. In comparison, Chinese companies have so far largely relied on homegrown talent. Hiring in the U.S. reflects a strategic shift by Chinese companies as they look to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets, experts said.

“Wanting to establish research teams in Silicon Valley makes perfect sense for Chinese AI companies seeking access to talent and the latest developments in the industry,” Cheryl Wu, a researcher in the economics of AI at Yale University and global think tank GovAI, told Rest of World.

Good Work and $$$

More than half of the world’s top AI researchers complete their undergraduate studies in China, a September study by research center Carnegie China said, based on the educational backgrounds of people who published papers at NeurIPS, one of the world’s leading AI conferences.

Yet the U.S. remains a global magnet for AI talent, the study concluded.

In 2025, the U.S. saw a net gain of 2,145 researchers while China recorded a net loss of 1,729, according to the analysis. 

China’s AI companies have been trying to lure top Chinese researchers at American AI labs to return home. One high-profile example is Tencent, which recruited former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu to lead its AI research.

Chinese companies are seeking “little geniuses” who have worked at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, a headhunter recruiting for Chinese labs in the Bay Area told Rest of World, requesting anonymity as she is not authorized to speak to the media.

These attempts, however, have not had much success because Chinese companies often struggle to match the salaries paid by their Silicon Valley peers.

“It’s money. Chinese companies simply don’t have enough of it to offer competitive wages for talent,” said Wu, who published a report examining Chinese AI companies’ financing with research institute Epoch AI. “They have only recently begun raising more substantial funding and still lag far behind their U.S. competitors.”

There is a stark gap between what Chinese and American AI companies pay employees.

MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, equivalent to roughly $203,000 per person, based on its year-end head count of 415, according to its financial filings. The annualized remuneration costs of Z.AI, another Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI lab, in the first half of 2026 amounted to $140,000 per employee. Neither company disclosed a breakdown of pay for engineers or researchers, and both figures include share-based compensation and staff across all departments.

In comparison, OpenAI advertises annual base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for research engineers in San Francisco, before equity awards. Three Chinese researchers working in Silicon Valley say it’s common for their peers to get an annual compensation package worth more than $1 million.

As of September, China’s six leading AI firms collectively generated only about 10% of the combined AI-related revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Wu’s research.

“Career prospects are another factor. Even senior Meta engineers might accept a lower-ranking position to join Anthropic because of its work on frontier AI,” Wu said. “That makes it even harder to persuade top talent to join a lab whose models are just not at the cutting edge.”

Chinese tech companies are now ramping up their salary game. If an AI researcher had offers from OpenAI or Anthropic, ByteDance’s frontier model division Seed would try to lure them with a competing offer that’s 1.5 times higher, according to a person familiar with the team.

Wu Yonghui, a veteran AI researcher who worked at Google for 17 years, joined Seed as the head of research in early 2025. Seed currently lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego, and Seattle. 

But even with matching pay, three Chinese researchers working in the U.S. told Rest of World they preferred American companies for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models. 

“I think most of the top Chinese talent would feel pretty comfortable in Silicon Valley; it’s the only other place where “996” isn’t really frowned upon,” Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, told Rest of World, referring to the demanding work culture common in China’s tech industry, where employees work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.

Extension of the U.S.-China AI war

Washington has spent years restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced Nvidia chips, and is scrutinizing their use of overseas data centers and cloud services. But no comparable restrictions prevent Chinese AI companies from establishing U.S. operations and hiring engineers there. 

Both Washington and Beijing are increasingly seeking to protect their most advanced AI technologies from each other.

The Chinese government proposed export controls on some of the country’s most advanced AI models, particularly those trained using the country’s “important data,” despite specifications.

U.S. officials and American AI companies, meanwhile, have accused Chinese AI labs of using unauthorized distillation techniques to replicate their models’ capabilities. On other sensitive tech fronts, like the semiconductor industry, the U.S. has already restricted some American engineers from working in Chinese facilities without a license.

While neither country has imposed a blanket ban on AI companies hiring researchers across borders, the growing competition over advanced technology could make talent recruitment another flashpoint.

“Given it is already so competitive, it doesn’t take much to imagine U.S. companies at some point capitalizing on U.S.-China competition and making national security arguments that will make it more difficult for Chinese labs to operate or to attract the best talent. Conversely, it’d be a similar dynamic if U.S. labs were operating in China,” Ma said. “This elite talent is by definition scarce; we are talking [about] like the top 5%–10% of people. Who wouldn’t want to hoard the best and the brightest for themselves?”

Chinese tech companies have previously faced U.S. restrictions that disrupted their American research operations. In 2019, telecom giant Huawei cut more than 600 jobs at its U.S. research arm, Futurewei, after Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist.

Not all Chinese AI companies want to hire in the U.S. China’s AI poster child, DeepSeek, continues to advertise research and engineering positions in China. It recently announced about 150 positions for engineers who would expand AI agentic and back-end infrastructure. In a 2024 interview, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said he hired mostly Chinese-educated people and believed the company itself could cultivate elite AI researchers.

Yale researcher Wu is skeptical that Chinese startups could attract enough top researchers to compete with America’s leading AI labs. “They may have plans to hire, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll be able to find the people,” she said.

entry.title: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
entry.summary: Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.
entry.content:
By Hsiuwen Liu and Peiyi Yu

Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.

About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in October, the first in the island’s semiconductor industry, after their union and the chipmaker failed to reach an agreement on salaries and bonuses. Their one-day action, while largely symbolic, is a reflection of the growing discontent among laborers in the artificial intelligence industry over how profits are distributed.  

The leading American memory chipmaker has posted record profits this year on the back of surging demand for AI chips. Unions representing workers at Micron’s facilities in Taoyuan and Taichung have been negotiating with the company for months for a profit-sharing agreement similar to those reached by employees at rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea.

“Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit instead of this unequal distribution between high-level executives and the rank and file,” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union, told Rest of World.

The global tech industry is heavily reliant on Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. Idaho-based Micron, the world’s third-biggest memory chipmaker, employs more than 15,000 workers in Taiwan. They produce over 60% of the company’s dynamic random access memory chips, used in AI servers. A prolonged workers’ strike could severely disrupt already strained supplies of memory chips worldwide.

Micron on October 22 said it had reached an agreement with the Taichung union for higher salaries and quarterly bonuses, and bigger contributions to the pension accounts of all workers at its Taiwan operations. But many union members rejected the deal, which they said was made in secret, while the majority of members of the Taoyuan union said they were dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement. 

“We do not accept the deal. None of our demands were fulfilled,” a Taoyuan union member, who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak to the media, told Rest of World. “We are surprised that the Taichung union representatives signed the deal.” 

The Taoyuan union, which is registered as a separate entity with more than 2,300 members, can still go on strike. 

Micron respects the workers’ “lawful rights and the applicable legal process,” a spokesperson for the company told Rest of World. “We are committed to constructive engagement with the Taoyuan and Taichung unions to reach a solution that works for all parties.”

Heightened consumer concern

Labor disputes and strikes in Taiwan have historically been associated with traditional industries. The actions by the Micron workers’ unions signal a broader shift as semiconductor workers increasingly organize to demand greater transparency and a fairer share of the value they help create, Wu Yu-ren, a labor relations professor at National Chung Cheng University, told Rest of World.

Over the past few months, membership in Micron’s two worker unions has surged from around 440 to more than 13,000. Earlier this year, employees of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. — which makes about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models — also discussed unionizing and striking over pay.

Taiwan’s high-tech companies have traditionally used generous benefits and bonuses to discourage workers from forming unions. White-collar tech workers have tended to change jobs instead of seeking collective action.

Now, “soaring demand for high-end memory has driven up share prices and corporate profits, making workers question how those gains are distributed,” Wu said. “The labor actions of Samsung and SK Hynix have also influenced the unionization of Taiwan tech workers.”

Across the world, policymakers, economists, and civil society groups are grappling with the widening gap between those who are benefiting from the AI boom and those who are being left behind. U.S. startups alone have created 19 billionaires worth a combined $59 billion over the past year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 

The Micron workers’ actions come as American frontier AI company Anthropic prepares to launch what could be the world’s biggest initial public offering, valuing the company at nearly $2 trillion. Its founders, investors, and some employees stand to become very wealthy.

In Taiwan, negotiations between Micron’s Taoyuan union and the company are continuing. In the event of another strike, the impact of a brief stop in production would likely be limited if backup personnel are available for equipment maintenance, process monitoring, and troubleshooting, Ellie Wang, an analyst at consulting firm TrendForce, told Rest of World. 

“The main consequence would be heightened customer concern over delivery reliability,” she said.

But if worker discontent spreads to other facilities or if there are prolonged strikes, it could disrupt supplies to downstream AI hardware makers such as Nvidia, and drive up prices. It would also hurt Taiwan’s wider economy, with the semiconductor sector making up more than a fifth of gross domestic product.

The stakes are high. Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, attended Micron’s opening ceremony for its new plant in Taichung last month, and urged the company and its workers to reach an agreement. “Corporations and employees should help each other like fish and water,” he said.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Labor said it would provide assistance and facilitate further dialogue between Micron and the Taoyuan union. “We hope that both parties will be willing to negotiate, reach a consensus as soon as possible and bring the dispute to an end,” it said in a statement. 

Building a constructive labor-management relationship before disputes escalate will be a challenge for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Pan Shih-wei, a former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor, told Rest of World. “Taiwan has traditionally relied on government intervention for labor disputes, and companies lack established channels for dialogue with workers.” 

The Micron dispute could lead to a wider labor movement as younger workers become more conscious of their rights, Pan said. 

“High-tech companies really need to take a closer look at how they manage labor relations,” he said. “Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common. … Ultimately, determining the profit-sharing ratio requires negotiations and engagement between the parties.”

entry.title: Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West
entry.summary: A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.
entry.content:
By Rina Chandran and Viola Zhou

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

The concept of machine unlearning — or removing data from an artificial intelligence system after it has been trained — was largely an academic pursuit when Ben Luria, an Israeli entrepreneur, co-founded his startup. Then, China’s DeepSeek launched its first open-weight large language model last year, and Luria immediately saw the business potential of realigning it to Western values.

A slew of Chinese open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.AI, AlibabaiAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.READ MORE, and TencentiTencentBest known for its super-app WeChat, Tencent is a Chinese technology conglomerate and a major player in the video gaming industry.READ MORE have won over users — including American businesses and startups — with their lower costs, strong capabilities, and customization options. Others fear the models are too aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, and that they are not as safe as closed systems.

“What we’re trying to do is find a way to de-risk the adoption of open-weight models,” Luria, co-founder and chief executive of AI safety startup Hirundo, told Rest of World. “What we do is like neurosurgery, an intervention that’s surgical and very specific. It is to realign the values, geopolitical perceptions, censorship, and state-aligned bias and propaganda to what American and Western companies expect from models they deploy in their workflows.” 

Luria’s team edits the weights of open models to harden them and make them more secure against cyberattacks, increase their fairness, and reduce their dangerous knowledge of, for example, bio weapons, he said. 

Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike’s analysis of DeepSeek’s R1 model last year showed that prompts containing topics the Chinese government considers politically sensitive were up to 50% more likely to receive code with “severe security vulnerabilities.” Another study found that Chinese models produced less secure code when the user identified as a member of the U.S. government.  

Hirundo’s own analysis of Alibaba’s Qwen models showed they do not acknowledge politically sensitive topics in China such as the violent crackdown on protests at Tiananmen Square in 1989 and Hong Kong in 2019, or the existence of forced labor camps in Xinjiang. They also don’t engage on prompts about Winnie the Pooh, possibly because dissidents have used the cartoon character to refer to Premier Xi Jinping.

Hirundo’s realignment ensures Chinese open models give “the balanced perspective” that OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude give, Luria said.

“We’re not making the model anti-Chinese,” he said. “We are bringing it up to speed on safety and to the standard of mainstream Western AI.”

“More palatable”

The top Chinese models lag behind the leading closed systems of U.S. frontier labs by just 3% on benchmark scores, and account for the biggest share of downloads on hosting platform Hugging Face as more developers use them. Companies including Airbnb, Uber, and legal AI firm Harvey have also built proprietary models on top of Chinese models, while Europe is developing its OpenEuroLLM sovereign AI model on Qwen. 

Yet concerns remain. In October, the Trump administration barred civilian government agencies from using products or services from DeepSeek, citing a potential threat to national security. 

Boston-based Lazarus AI, which deploys on-premise AI services for the U.S. government and highly regulated industries, realigned Alibaba’s Qwen models by removing their mandatory censorship. It identified the banned topics from leaked censorship guidelines, then generated prompts related to those topics, and used answers produced by Google’s Gemini Flash to realign the models.

After the intervention, the models were able to give information that was not in the training materials, such as names of pro-democracy activists, suggesting the models had originally learned such knowledge and were suppressed from expressing it, Eric Hartford, former chief scientist at Lazarus AI, told Rest of World.

“In the United States, we have this fear of Chinese models potentially having dangerous behaviors baked into them,” he said. “My goal was to … present these models to enterprises and to highly regulated industries and to have [the models] be palatable for them.”

The company’s ReAligned models, billed as “open-source frontier models without the propaganda,” have been deployed at about a dozen companies in the U.S., Hartford said. But other clients, including government agencies, are reluctant to adopt Chinese models even though they are more capable than the open-weight models from OpenAI and Thinking Machines Lab, which they prefer, he said. 

“An impossible standard”

While companies such as Hirundo and Lazarus say their method is effective, aligning a model to so-called Western values or making it universally safe “is an impossible standard,” Oriane Peter, a Ph.D. researcher in AI at King’s College London, told Rest of World.

Alignment is about “steering a model’s output toward a specific desired behavior within a well-defined cultural context and application,” she said.

So anyone using a Chinese model outside China must realign it, “not because Western ideology is inherently safer, or more ethical, but because any model must be adapted to the specific social context and environment in which it is meant to operate,” Peter said.

As Chinese open-weight models are widely adopted, there are more tools that claim to uncensor them and remove their refusal mechanisms, a process called abliteration. But many of these tools are not effective, and the models can still retain some of the censorship and misinformation, Luria said.

“It shows that the alignments are deeply embedded, and it’s not that simple to get rid of them.”

Worldwide, there is growing pushback against Western bias in AI systems, with even some Chinese and Russian models defaulting to American geopolitical narratives on historical events, according to researchers. Countries across Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East are developing sovereign AI models to better reflect their languages and culture.

Silicon Valley’s centralized control over model alignment can lead to “a massive homogenization effect” in AI systems, said Peter. This has been linked to cognitive homogenization and intellectual decline among users.

Most users of Chinese models do not care about their alignment, Graham Webster, editor-in-chief of the DigiChina Project at Stanford University, said at a recent Rest of World event.

“If I were running a product in Taiwan, I would be more concerned because it would be throughput that is potentially relevant to the stuff that the Chinese government has enforced strict control over in the training data and the training,” he said. “But if I’m making a product that helps people make a website for their coffee shop, it doesn’t matter.”

Stu Clott, a developer in San Diego, uses DeepSeek for writing, research, and coding tasks. He does not see the need for a realigned model, he told Rest of World.

“I have not had a single situation where censorship got in my way,” he said.

entry.title: Why Africa needs its own AI off switch
entry.summary: Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.
entry.content:
By Jane Munga

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Imagine that it is 6 a.m. in the wholesale markets of Nairobi. Merchants are delivering vegetables from up-country farms to the retailers who sell to the city’s households. Everyone is using M-Pesa, Safaricom’s mobile money platform, when suddenly, the system crashes, bringing the market to a standstill. Imagine that across the continent in Accra, MTN’s MoMo has also crashed, and business in Makola Market has all but stopped.

With the growing number of cyberattacks caused by artificial intelligence, these are highly plausible scenarios. In both these cases, Safaricom, MTN, and the Kenyan and Ghanaian governments need an off switch, or the technical ability and know-how to stop a rogue AI agent from executing its code on their payment systems.

Currently, the conversation on AI agents revolves around China versus the U.S., open versus closed models, and who will dominate the AI race. But in Africa’s capitals, the distinction that will ultimately matter is not whose product was used to build a system, or who dominates whom, but rather whether AI can serve its purpose and be controlled locally. So how can Africa build with agency, and with control over the code and makeup of its own systems, even though they are built on foreign technology?

African countries are already building AI for digital transformation, as outlined in the African Union’s continental AI strategy and country-specific AI strategies. Policymakers are building AI infrastructure but rarely discuss how AI delivers economic growth in a safe environment. Developers across Africa are creating AI-powered innovations that sit on the continent’s digital infrastructure — chief among them is mobile money. These innovations bring new opportunities, but also new threats. In July, AI agents running inside an OpenAI evaluation attacked the production infrastructure of Hugging Face. In September, rogue OpenAI agents breached Australian government websites. Africa, the home of mobile money, which has brought financial inclusion to hundreds of millions, may be the next target.

In countries like Kenya and Ghana, mobile money is not simply another digital service; it is infrastructure for everyday economic activity. It is how small traders receive payments, households move money, and bills are settled. The scale is significant: More than $2 trillion flowed through mobile money globally in 2025, of which $1.4 trillion, roughly two-thirds, was transacted in sub-Saharan Africa. East Africa alone accounted for $806 billion and West Africa for $498 billion. An agent capable of disrupting transactions, manipulating accounts, or disabling access at scale could therefore disrupt livelihoods and economic activity very quickly, and a single point of failure can have outsize effects, with far-reaching consequences for people who have little to fall back on.

Small-scale traders mostly live on what they sell each day, rarely have credit, and in most African societies lack robust social welfare to cushion the loss. For a trader in Nairobi or Accra, losing a day’s income would be devastating, and the disruption can run back up the chain to farmers, and to the households and families who depend on the market.

So how do we protect it?

Building differently

The answer lies in how Africa builds its AI systems, and who controls them. Whether a rogue agent can simply be switched off depends on how the AI model is deployed. If it runs on a centrally controlled cloud service, the provider may be able to revoke access, disable credentials, or shut the system down; that is the closed-model case. If the underlying model is an open-weight one that has been downloaded, modified, and deployed independently across multiple systems, containment becomes much harder. The loss of control is therefore less about a machine suddenly becoming omnipotent and more about humans losing the ability to understand, interrupt, or reverse actions occurring across interconnected systems quickly enough.

African developers are building largely on open models, which are arguably cheaper and can be run locally. But they present a trade-off: Open models give developers more control over their own systems, but less protection when someone else misuses them. Closed models carry a cost of their own. When Hugging Face investigated the July intrusion, it had to run the forensic analysis on a Chinese open-weight model because the U.S. models blocked requests containing real attack code. The same central control that lets a closed model be switched off also constrains the people defending against it. This means both open- and closed-weight models carry their own vulnerabilities that must be addressed when building Africa’s AI economy.

This means building differently, beginning with partnerships that position Africa as a technology developer and not only a consumer, and through which it builds its own capability to design systems where the user is in control. Such partnerships are essential to ensure that the end user, and the state, retain control over access, and that dependency is not recreated. This also moves the narrative toward building African AI not around the U.S. or China but around avoiding lock-in to a single vendor or stack. The goal is solutions built with agency, which use imported technologies to develop homegrown solutions, with applications that are robust and equipped with the necessary security measures.

Those security measures are how Africa should insulate itself from crippling disruptions. African countries have limited cybersecurity and incident-response capacity, and they depend on foreign providers. So another key issue is capacity: Do African governments and firms have the monitoring systems, technical expertise, and redundancy needed to detect an autonomous system behaving unexpectedly and contain it quickly? Hugging Face detected and contained its intrusion, but its own automated systems initially failed to escalate the alert. It is one of the best-resourced AI companies in the world. Very few African public or private institutions have anything close to that capability. Africa must build its own cybersecurity defenses fit for the agentic AI age.

Building them demands a refocus in African AI policy, so that it treats resilience as seriously as adoption. As governments digitize and build AI on critical systems, they need human override mechanisms, segmentation, auditability, incident response, and credible offline fallbacks designed in from the beginning. That is the off switch, and on the day that M-Pesa and MoMo crash, it has to be in the hands of those who are responsible for protecting their citizens and their platforms.

entry.title: AI models cost more when you don’t use English
entry.summary: Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.
entry.content:
By Ananya Bhattacharya

Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.

People who use less widely spoken languages could end up paying more to use artificial intelligence than those who speak English or other dominant languages.

A new study published last month by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found AI models require far more tokens for some languages than others. Tokens are the units of text or data that the models process. The researchers have called this a hidden “tokenizer tax,” which can make AI more expensive in languages with smaller online presence. A tokenizer is a tool that breaks down raw text, images, or audio into tokens.

Even within the 20 most popular languages on the internet, there is a gap in token usage, the research found. The most expensive of the languages used between 1.5 and 5 times more tokens than the cheapest. This gap widened when researchers expanded the set to 200 languages, with the token cost gap in one AI model growing by 17 times.

“A startup in [Bengaluru] may pay a surcharge on every prompt and completion while its competitor in Austin does not,” the study said. “The tokenizer tax also has implications beyond cost. Higher token counts translate into higher latency and reduced effective context capacity. These penalties hit hardest where compute and connectivity are already limited. Tokenizer inequity is a constraint on who can participate in the AI economy.”

Non-English languages leave less room for documents or conversation history, and require more work to generate the answer, according to Pratyush Choudhury, co-founder of Activate AI, India’s first venture capital fund dedicated exclusively to AI. Activate backs multilingual voice AI startups like ElevenLabs, Sarvam, and Wispr Flow.

“Think about a tutor: Retaining the student’s earlier mistakes and explanations is part of delivering a good lesson. If that history consumes the context window much faster in one language, the disadvantage reaches into the quality of the service,” he said.

One way to improve language processing is to improve the underlying data.

“Open data efforts matter here, like RESPIN, a collaborative initiative with [the Indian Institute of Science] funded by the Gates Foundation, where we collected text from native speakers of 38 dialects along with read speech,” Raoul Nanavati, co-founder and CEO of Mumbai-based AI voice infrastructure startup Navana.ai, told Rest of World. 

However, the study by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found the rarity of a language isn’t the only determinant of how many tokens it uses. The script plays a big role. 

Asturian, which has relatively few speakers and no Common Crawl data, “benefits from the Latin-script advantage, as well as the representation from other related Romance languages like Italian,” while languages written in scripts the tokenizer rarely saw — Burmese, Tibetan, Tifinagh, Khmer, Lao, and Ol Chiki — were at the greatest disadvantage consistently across nearly all models in the analysis.

Many tokenizers today remain disproportionately optimized for English and other high-resource languages, and the underlying issue is the lack of high-quality digital data, said Dheemanth Reddy, CEO of Maya Research, which is developing conversational AI models designed to speak and respond like native speakers for the next 5 billion internet users. But better training data alone doesn’t fix the tokenizer, he warned.

“Token prices are falling very quickly, so the direct cost impact should become less severe over time, and better multilingual and synthetic data should improve model quality. But actually fixing the tokenization gap will still require labs to deliberately design future tokenizers to handle these languages and scripts better,” Reddy said.

Choudhury said language efficiency should be a product requirement, alongside accuracy, speed, and reliability. 

“Perfect equality may be unrealistic. Large, persistent disparities should still require an explanation and an improvement plan,” he said. “I would ask every major lab to publish a language-by-language scorecard showing what it costs to complete comparable tasks successfully, and commit to measurable improvements for its worst-served languages.”

entry.title: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
entry.summary: In his new book “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” writer Paris Marx examines how local communities are resisting the growing demand for water to cool data centers.
entry.content:
By Paris Marx

In his new book “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” writer Paris Marx examines how local communities are resisting the growing demand for water to cool data centers.

After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.

That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.

As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.

A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.

The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.

Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.

If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago. 

The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare. 

Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.

According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.

The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.

The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.

After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water. 

Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.

Vicente Bardales, a member of the Quilicura Socio Environmental Resistance group, told Rest of World that the companies touch down in places like Quilicura only to “use water, [and] dry up the territory, but don’t give anything back to the population.” 

Similar scenarios to that of Chile played out across Latin America. The following year, the Uruguayan capital of Montevideo found itself under a state of emergency as the country was hit by its worst drought in 70 years. As residents demonstrated against the misuse of water by industry, they found out Google was planning a data center in Canelones, a little less than an hour north of Montevideo.

“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption,” explained Daniel Pena, a researcher at University of the Republic. “The majority is used for big agro industries, such as soya, rice, and wood pulping. Now we have Google planning to use enormous quantities of water.” Pena had to go to court to get details of its planned water use from the Ministry of Environment, ultimately finding Google’s 72-acre site was planning to use 2 million gallons of water each day to power its cooling systems.

Uruguayans had fought for fresh drinking water to be considered a basic right in the national constitution two decades earlier, and as companies like Google moved in, they feared its realization was slipping from their grasp.

Uruguayans suspected Google had shifted its focus to their country because it had run into such opposition in Chile. Neighboring Brazil already has over 180 data centers, even as many regions regularly experience drought conditions. On the outskirts of Fortaleza, Brazil’s fourth-largest city, at least four major data centers were looking to set up shop to take advantage of a free-trade zone in the municipality of Caucaia. One in particular would be the size of 12 football fields, costing an estimated $10 billion, and though it will technically be owned by a local wind energy company, it is actually being developed to serve TikTok. This is in a region that experienced emergency drought conditions for 16 of the 21 years between 2003 and 2024.

What Cerillos, Canelones, and Caucaia are experiencing is increasingly a global phenomenon. Around the world, data center companies claim they will be respectful and considerate neighbors, but too often they hide the extent of the damage that follows from the scale of their demands on local resources. This is particularly acute in parts of the Global South, but the effects are now also being felt across the United States and Europe.

Adapted from “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires” by Paris Marx published by Riverhead Books, an imprint of Penguin Random House © 2026 by Paris Marx, and reprinted with permission.

entry.title: Will developing nations be able to handle millions of AI agents?
entry.summary: It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.
entry.content:
By Danai Nesta Kupemba

It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.

Big Tech’s newest personal agents — Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots — promise to book tables at restaurants, buy groceries, and carry out other types of digital grunt work for users.

Consumers are opting in. Muse has been downloaded 9 million times in the U.S. and Canada since its launch on September 8, market intelligence company AppMagic, told Rest of World. As many as 1.8 million people use the app daily. 

Meta aspires to a global launch. “[We] are quite excited to bring personal agents to billions of people around the world,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, told the Financial Times.

Some startups are already building agents in markets that Big Tech hopes to reach. For instance, South African startup ManyHands offers Manny, a personal assistant designed to order groceries, book appointments and make payments through WhatsApp. But adapting agents to local conditions has its challenges. Anton Moulder, ManyHands’ founder, told Rest of World that getting the AI assistant to converse in all of South Africa’s 11 official spoken languages has been difficult.

Rest of World spoke to AI researchers and other experts to understand how these personal agents would perform outside Western nations.

Would AI agents understand the local language and culture?

English speakers could benefit more from AI agents, which run on top of large language models that underperform in many non-English languages. 

“Linguistic inclusion is ultimately about power,” Payal Arora, professor of inclusive AI cultures at Utrecht University and the founder of Inclusive AI Lab, told Rest of World.

Meta has said that expanding Muse internationally would require support for local languages and integration with local services.

AI agents would also need to understand the local culture, including the unique ways people communicate and bargain. “In many parts of the Global South, meaning is deeply contextual, shaped by family, community, religion, local institutions, and informal social networks,” Arora said.

Without that understanding, agents might impose Western assumptions on their users, Usha Raman, an independent researcher on AI policy and digital culture, told Rest of World. “The danger then is that existing forms of cultural and economic hegemony continue and the rest of the world is forced to adapt,” she said.

What happens when millions of agents go online?

Agents searching and completing transactions for millions of people could stress networks and websites. “Internet connectivity may be poor [in developing nations], affecting not only the user’s interaction with AI, but what agents can do online,” Kentaro Toyama, professor of community information at the University of Michigan, told Rest of World.

A single task given to an agent can trigger repeated exchanges between the agent, its AI model, and different websites. Cisco describes agents as “network power users,” generating up to 450% more traffic per task than a human in its testing. Agent traffic is growing online: Daily requests from AI agents on Cloudflare’s network increased by more than 1,700% over the past year.

Rising traffic wouldn’t immediately affect regions that have spare network capacity, such as East Africa, Kyle Spencer, executive director of the African IXP Association, told Rest of World. But other places with poor networks, such as Niger, Burkina Faso, or eastern Congo, could face problems, he said.

The bigger challenge would be keeping connections reliable. Road construction often damages fiber cables, Spencer said. The network could also get disrupted if undersea cables bringing internet into a nation get damaged.

Though Muse and Dots could continue working as they are cloud-based, they may be unable to reach necessary services. They also wouldn’t be able to reach users who lose connectivity for instructions or approvals to complete a task.

Could personal agents widen Africa’s digital divide?

Only 36% of Africans used the internet in 2025, compared to 92% of Europeans and 88% of North and South Americans, according to the International Telecommunication Union. City dwellers in Africa were 2.6 times more likely to use the internet than people who live in the countryside.

“If agents were to work in Africa, they might unfortunately deepen inequality,” Jane Munga, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Rest of World.

The cost of accessing agents could also limit who benefits, Munga said. Though Muse can be accessed for free, many other agents are paid. Dots is available for a minimum of $100 a month. “These are costs that most Global South users may not be in a position to absorb,” she said.

How would local businesses need to rewire for AI agents?

Local businesses would have to make their websites understandable, readable, and usable by bots. If they do not, they risk losing out on digital economic opportunities.

This would be challenging for small, offline businesses, such as a vendor at a vegetable market. They would have to go online, maintain an inventory, know how much stock they own, and create ways for bots to pay, Munga said. This requires money and skills.

Businesses may also have to invest more in customer support. “Agents might purchase more, and request more returns — when human users decide agents erred — putting stress on businesses,” said Toyama.

Could regulators hold agents accountable?

Agents perform better the more they know the user, Mercy King’ori, policy manager for Africa at the Future of Privacy Forum, told Rest of World. A user’s favorite restaurants, shops, and regularly visited places could help an agent build a picture of their tastes, habits, and daily life.

“An agent may draw conclusions about a person or a group, such as their likely income, health, creditworthiness, or behaviour from the data it handles,” King’ori said.

In cases where agents are developed and hosted outside the country, regulators may be unable to supervise the systems, said King’ori.

entry.title: Western open-weight models still can’t beat China
entry.summary: Chinese open-weight AI models offer high capability at significantly lower costs than U.S. frontier systems, but face monetization and compute challenges, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.
entry.content:
By Rina Chandran

Chinese open-weight AI models offer high capability at significantly lower costs than U.S. frontier systems, but face monetization and compute challenges, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.

A slew of new open-weight artificial intelligence models from American and European companies aim to convert users of Chinese open models who are concerned about security, but fall short of the dominant Chinese systems on performance despite having greater resources, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.   

Last week, American startup Reflection launched its first open-weight model, and European labs Aleph Alpha and Mistral also released new open-weight models. Open models such as these offer users greater customization and control than the closed models of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google at significantly lower costs.

For businesses and governments in lower-income countries, in particular, cost is the primary factor, as well as the expertise needed to customize open models for their specific needs, including in areas such as education, healthcare, and farming, Daniel Björkegren, an assistant professor at Columbia University, said at the Rest of World event last week.

“In the low-income context, there’s a lot of concern about being dependent on the U.S. for frontier intelligence,” he said. “American models are also very tuned for American workloads, but when you take those same models and try to deploy them in remote parts of the world, often they don’t work so well.”

Users, particularly businesses, switch models “when new capabilities and lower prices emerge,” Björkegren said. But “one enduring question is, how easy is it to switch?”

Since the launch of DeepSeek early last year, Chinese open models have rapidly closed in on their U.S. rivals. A growing number of U.S. startups and businesses, as well as the European Union’s sovereign AI project, use them. The OpenRouter leaderboard of large language models had four Chinese models among its top five last week — DeepSeek, Z.ai, XiaomiiXiaomiXiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales.READ MORE, and TencentiTencentBest known for its super-app WeChat, Tencent is a Chinese technology conglomerate and a major player in the video gaming industry.READ MORE. LiveBench, which ranks models on various benchmarks, recently had DeepSeek in the top five for the first time, and showed that the top Chinese models lagged behind their U.S. rivals by just 3% on benchmark scores.

Critical to China’s ambition

China’s leader Xi Jinping has described open models as key to the country’s ambition to shape the development of the technology, and reach its goal of “global AI leadership” by 2030. This year, China established the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization to promote AI adoption and shape AI governance in developing nations. That includes access to Chinese models, and training for students and workers.

China’s plan for economic progress is through innovation, and open-weight models give it an opportunity to get around some of the concerns about its presence in overseas markets, Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the independent AI safety and security program MATS, said at the Rest of World event.

“China has, for a long time, talked about open innovation and contributing to global innovation, and they weren’t able to do that because in some cases, like Huawei, the U.S. pushed back,” she said. “With open models, because people can download them and use them and own them, it’s private to them — so you kind of break down the trust problem when it comes to concern over the Chinese state.”

“It’s good for soft power. It’s good domestically, as well,” Loke said.

The directive from the U.S. government to Anthropic earlier this year to suspend access to its Fable 5 and Mythos models for all foreign nationals on national security grounds also reinforced to several governments that they should not depend entirely on American systems, Björkegren said.

“If your digital infrastructure is dependent on a foreign country, and for geopolitical reasons access could be pulled, that is really problematic,” he said. “Strategically, a government is going to be in a better position if there are more providers from different countries that have diverse interests, so that you’re not going to be subject to a holdup problem.”

A growing number of instances of AI agents at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta hacking websites and taking other unauthorized actions has shifted the narrative around open models being less safe. Hugging Face said it used a Chinese open-weight model while  defending itself from a swarm of AI agents from OpenAI because American models refused its prompts.

Trade restrictions that limit China’s access to the most advanced chips from Nvidia have forced Chinese companies to build more efficient models that require less computing power. American open models from Meta, Nvidia, and others do not come close in capability, Graham Webster, a research scholar and editor-in-chief at the DigiChina Project at Stanford University, said at the Rest of World event.

“If you need relatively frontier capability, right now that’s Chinese open models only,” he said. “If there were U.S.-made open models that were at such high performance as the Chinese open models, you might observe whether people had a preference for a U.S.-made open model. But you don’t see that because the U.S. companies just don’t release those.”

“Competition is hard“

Last week, as Reflection announced the launch of its first open-weight model, Nathan Lambert, head of AI research lab Trillium Labs, wrote on X: “Reflection joins the list of Nvidia & Thinking Machines who have released their strongest models and come up behind Chinese counterparts. There’s a lot of ways people will overthink this, but the clearest takeaway should be that the Chinese are very very good at building LLMs.”

When the head of product at Reflection responded that it was their first product, Lambert wrote: “The point is that some of the best and most funded researchers in the U.S. may not win. Competition is hard.”

Still, Chinese AI companies are grappling with compute limits and the question of how to make money. Their open models can do some tasks 50% to 90% cheaper than the leading American frontier models. Moonshot AI is negotiating revenue-sharing deals with Microsoft, Amazon, and Google to host its Kimi K3 model — a rare deal between a Chinese AI firm and U.S. cloud providers.

The Chinese government will be keen to maintain the lead, Webster said.

“The government would prefer that China be home to the leading open-weight model,” he said. “They can throw more money at things, but you can only buy so many chips under current conditions. The Chinese companies have been doing a very good job of figuring out how to do more with less. But they may run into a wall.”

Monetization is a question that concerns every Chinese AI company, Loke said. “The hope is to get as much traction and adoption, and that once people like your model enough, hopefully, they stick with you,” she said.

For the government, enabling Chinese open models to thrive locally and globally is critical. “Strategically, it makes a lot of sense for them to win hearts and minds, win markets,” Loke said.

entry.title: What the West can learn from AI optimists in the rest of the world
entry.summary: The developing world’s enthusiastic adoption of AI and necessity-driven innovations offer lessons for an anxiety-ridden West.
entry.content:
By Payal Arora

The developing world’s enthusiastic adoption of AI and necessity-driven innovations offer lessons for an anxiety-ridden West.

On a recent Sunday afternoon, I was invited to debate AI’s impact on the cultural sector alongside Dutch politicians and creative-industry leaders. I was the lone optimist, arguing that if fear and risk become our primary lens for governing artificial intelligence, we will design systems around what we want to prevent rather than what we want to use them for. Then I said something that was harder for the room to hear: The Global South is home to some of AI’s most enthusiastic and inventive users, and their experiments could help us rethink our own institutions. 

The U.S. is no different from Europe. A culture of fear encourages protectionism: We hunker down and romanticize legacy systems rather than ask what might replace them. Creative industries in the majority world have spent decades navigating piracy and weak enforcement, forcing them to think beyond rights-based policing about how creators actually receive value. Anghami, the biggest music app in the Middle East, for instance, pays musicians from their first stream, rather than only after a song reaches a minimum threshold. It has approached AI pragmatically, using it to curate, tag, and attribute creative work rather than simply blocking and banning.

In the West, fear of AI has helped turn pessimism into a cultural virtue. Would you publicly say you love AI? Your answer may say something about where you’re from. Say “yes” to a concerned audience in the U.S. or the Netherlands, and you risk being seen as naive, or complicit in extraction and exploitation. While the U.S. is building and deploying AI at a scale no other country matches, Americans are deeply anxious about where it is heading. Only 17% of U.S. adults think AI will have a positive impact on the country over the next 20 years, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey. 

In much of the Global South, the mood is markedly different. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that 83% of respondents in China, 80% in Indonesia, and 77% in Thailand said AI-powered products offer more benefits than drawbacks, compared with 39% in the U.S. and 36% in the Netherlands. 

So why the divide?

It’s all about access

Demographics are a part of the answer. Nearly 90% of the world’s young people live outside the West. They are not simply using AI, they are playing with it. Drive through Hyderabad or Bengaluru and you will see billboards for AI crash courses and Bollywood films promoted as AI-made. I have spent two decades talking with young people from the rural Himalayas to the slums of Hyderabad, and they often tell me some version of the same thing: They love technology. Their enthusiasm is not necessarily about the technology itself, it is about what AI might democratize: access to institutions and opportunities that have long excluded people with the least social or cultural capital.

A founder I met in Gurgaon told me she is anxious about AI too, but that it has allowed her to reach clients far beyond the English-speaking world, reinventing her business in a fraction of the time it once took. A civic activist in Chennai taught herself to code with AI and built a gender violence-alert app in multiple languages, at a moment when funding for such work is drying up and state scrutiny is rising. Having seen what deepfake abuse does to women, she sees AI as one of the few tools powerful enough to fight back. India consistently ranks among the most optimistic countries on AI even as anxiety about jobs rises.

It would be easy for the West to dismiss these stories as products of scarcity, shaped by conditions far removed from our own. That would be a mistake. Constraint has a way of forcing people to rewrite the rules of the game. At a technology festival in Athens this year, creatives told me they worry AI might kill short filmmaking. In China, AI-made micro-dramas have become a multibillion-dollar industry. One breakout film, Zombie Cleaner, was made for less than $500 by a part-time wedding photographer in rural Yunnan province, and went on to attract tens of millions of views overseas. The significance is not the novelty of AI-generated entertainment. It is that AI lowers the cost of entering a cultural market. People in smaller Chinese cities can tell stories in their own accents and languages rather than waiting for mainstream media to tell them what counts as a story.

Building for need, not market share

A few months ago, I spoke to employees at a multinational company about “inclusive AI.” I was asked to remove a slide on AI’s potential harms because it might discourage adoption. That exchange captures something important about AI adoption in the West. Corporations increasingly pressure employees and customers to use AI, often because adoption itself has become a measure of competitiveness. The question is how to maximize market return.

Elsewhere, the question is more often: What problem can this solve?

Where capital and resources are scarce, technologies are frequently built around concrete public needs. India, with a fraction of Europe’s resources, built India Stack: a public digital infrastructure for identity, payments, and data-sharing that companies can build on rather than infrastructure controlled by a handful of private platforms. Europe is now looking to India’s example as it develops EuroStack, in response to the growing need for digital sovereignty.

Innovation does not always come from having more. Sometimes it comes from having less room for failure. The countries with the least room for error are experimenting with AI not because they are blind to its risks, but because they cannot afford to wait for perfect systems to solve chronic problems. The West should pay closer attention.

The point is not to romanticize the Global South, but to recognize that we have a remarkably narrow vision of what AI can be for. We ask whether it will replace workers, destroy creativity, undermine democracy, or kill our planet. These are necessary questions. But what if we also asked what AI could help us rebuild? Young people around the world are using it for work, entertainment, romance, creativity, activism, and self-expression. They are not waiting for institutions to tell them what the technology is supposed to be for.

If the most powerful builders keep designing for market share while the world’s most resource-constrained builders design for survival and self-actualization, the templates that spread globally for governance, infrastructure, and who gets to participate may increasingly come from wherever necessity did the inventing. The West is warning the world about what AI might do to us. Perhaps it is time to ask what the rest of the world might teach us to do with it.

entry.title: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes
entry.summary: China’s EV giant says a shortage of ships is holding back its exports.
entry.content:
By Indranil Ghosh

China’s EV giant says a shortage of ships is holding back its exports.

China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE is building cars faster than it can export, so it’s adding more ships.

The world’s largest electric vehicle maker will expand its fleet of car-carrying cargo ships to 18 from eight by 2029, according to shipping industry reports. Each new carrier will have the capacity to carry about 9,200 cars and will be built by China Merchants Industry.

Owning its fleet could cut BYD’s cost to ship each car abroad by as much as 40% compared with renting carriers, according to one industry estimate. BYD’s increasing export capacity could help it push further into global markets, intensifying competition for automakers including Tesla and traditional U.S. brands.

“Carmakers like BYD, which invested in the sector ahead of the surge, are reaping the rewards of that long-term strategy,” Andrea De Luca, a maritime analyst at Boston-based shipping data company Veson Nautical, told Rest of World. “By owning their ships, they can save money compared with chartering at today’s elevated rates, prioritize their most important markets, enter new ones more easily, and depend less on charter market swings.”

BYD did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment.

Why BYD owns ships

In 2022, BYD announced a plan worth $687 million to build its own car carriers, to fix what founder Wang Chuanfu called a shortage of shipping capacity for exports. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the company put eight car carriers into service.

Earlier this year, BYD told investors that a shortage of shipping capacity had held back its exports. In September, the company sold 180,700 cars outside China, more than double a year ago and almost 40% of its monthly total sales.

Wars in the Red Sea and around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up freight costs and forced ships onto longer routes around conflict zones. Renting a car carrier with capacity of about 6,500 cars now costs $95,000 a day, up from $50,000 in February, according to shipping data and analytics firm Clarksons Research. Chinese owners account for only about 10% of global car carrier capacity, including ships on order, so carmakers from the country hire ships from international shipping companies, the research arm of shipbroker Clarksons said.

With BYD aiming to sell more than 2.5 million cars overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year, owning a fleet cushions against higher shipping bills and gives more control over space and routes, analysts said.

2.5 million Number of cars BYD aims to sell overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year.

“The very strong growth in Chinese exports, fueling strong Asia-Europe fronthaul demand growth, is the biggest single factor behind the increase in charter rates,” Stephen Gordon, managing director of Clarksons Research, told Rest of World. “Additionally, conflict in the Middle East has caused regional disruption and inefficiencies, which have helped to further tighten markets after a two-year period of gradual normalization.”

Most car carriers on Asia-Europe routes are sailing around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Red Sea, adding about 25% to the distance and as many as 14 days to each voyage, De Luca said. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, the spot rate for moving cars from China to the Middle East has jumped to $220 per cubic meter of cargo space from $65 in February, he said.

Chinese EVs and exports

In China, industrywide sales of EVs and plug-in hybrids fell 12% in the first eight months of the year, after the government cut tax breaks for buyers. BYD sold 33% fewer cars at home over the same period.

Many Chinese carmakers have kept their factories busy by selling surplus cars abroad as changes to tax and subsidy incentives have cooled demand at home, George Whitcombe, a senior EV analyst at London-based battery data provider Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Rest of World.

Exports of China-made EVs are now rising faster than their registrations overseas, pointing to a growing stock of unsold cars, he said.

“Control over its distribution network is a strategy BYD has long pursued,” Whitcombe said. “With other Chinese automakers left without their own fleet of ships and exposed to rising shipping costs, it potentially leaves them in a less competitive position to grow their overseas presence.”

Tesla, BYD’s main U.S. rival, has relied on other companies’ carriers to export from China. Its Shanghai plant shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home in the first eight months of the year.
